# Fuel Retail: Pass-Through, Competition and Demand

<p style="font-family:'IBM Plex Mono',monospace; font-size:.8rem; letter-spacing:.02em;">
Error-correction model · Asymmetric pass-through · Fixed effects · Hierarchical forecasting · MinT · Gradient boosting · DuckDB · Delta Lake · Databricks · MLflow · Python · 10 tests
</p>
:::

::: {.rh-section}
## The business question

A fuel distributor and its network of stations live on three numbers: how fast the pump price
follows the cost, how much a brand and the stations around it allow a station to charge, and how
many litres each state will buy. The first is also a public question. Drivers suspect that prices
"go up like a rocket and come down like a feather", and regulators ask the same.

This case answers the three on public data, the way a data team would run it in production: from
the regulator's files to a bronze, silver and gold lakehouse, models tested out of time, and a
job ready for Databricks.
:::

::: {.rh-section}
## The data

All public, from ANP, Brazil's oil, gas and biofuels regulator:

* **The weekly retail price survey, station by station**: 4.2 million prices from 18,921 stations
  in 464 municipalities, January 2021 to June 2026, with each station's brand. The first half of
  2022 is not published.
* **Distribution prices**, weekly by state, since August 2020.
* **Producer and importer prices**, weekly by region, since 2013.
* **Sales**, monthly by state and product, since 1990.

The page groups brands into major brands, other brands and white flag; no distributor is named.
:::

::: {.rh-section}
## Try it

Pick a state and see its weekly prices and how fast the pump follows a cost rise and a cost fall;
move the distribution price and see the expected pump price week by week; compare all 27 states;
see what brand and nearby competitors are worth; and explore the twelve-month sales forecast of
each state, region and the country.

::: {.rh-section}
## Method, and why this one

**A lakehouse from the regulator's files.** DuckDB SQL turns the published files (two encodings,
decimal commas, several layouts over the years) into silver tables, and these into gold weekly
state series and municipality-week panels, written as Delta tables. A Databricks Asset Bundle runs
the same steps as a weekly job on Unity Catalog, and every run is logged to MLflow.

**Pass-through as an error-correction model.** For each state, the pump price and the
distribution price share a long-run relation; in the short run, cost rises and cost falls get
their own coefficients, and the gap to the long-run relation closes week by week (Engle and
Granger, 1987; Borenstein, Cameron and Gilbert, 1997). Symmetry is a Wald test on the sums of the
rise and fall coefficients, with Newey-West errors, and the 27 p-values are corrected for multiple
testing with Benjamini-Hochberg. The window is July 2022 to June 2026, the longest stretch with
continuous station data.

**Brand and competition within the same market.** Each station's price is compared with the mean of
its municipality in the same week, which removes local costs, taxes and the week's shocks; that
relative price is regressed on the brand group and on the number of surveyed competitors in the
same 5-digit postal code, with errors clustered by municipality.

**Forecasts that add up.** Monthly sales of gasoline C, hydrous ethanol and diesel are forecast for
Brazil, its 5 regions and 27 states with a seasonal naive benchmark, exponential smoothing (ETS)
and a global gradient-boosting model, at 12 origins from 2023 to 2025, 12 months ahead, refitting
on the past only. MinT (Wickramasuriya, Athanasopoulos and Hyndman, 2019) then makes the 33
forecasts of each product coherent: states add up to regions and regions to the country.
:::

::: {.rh-section}
## Result

**No rockets and feathers at the pump.** Symmetry is rejected at 5% in 4 of 27 states and in 2
after the correction for multiple testing, one where rises pass faster and one where falls do. In
15 states the short-run response is larger for rises, in 12 for falls. In São Paulo about half of
a change in the distribution price reaches the pump in the same week and all of it within two
weeks, in either direction. Where drivers see prices stick, the delay is upstream of the station.

**A brand is worth about 2%.** Within the same municipality and week, stations of the major brands
charge 2.1% more for regular gasoline than white-flag stations (95% interval 1.7% to 2.6%), and
other brands 1.1% more. More competitors nearby do not mean lower prices in this data: stations
with eleven or more surveyed competitors in their postal area charge 0.6% more, because dense areas
are city centres and highways. Prices spread more in big markets: the gap between the 90th and the
10th percentile station is R$ 0.22 per litre in municipalities with 5 to 9 stations and R$ 0.64 in
those with 50 or more.

**Forecasts: simple and coherent wins.** Mean error 12 months ahead (WAPE):

| Product | Level | Seasonal naive | ETS | ETS + MinT | Global GBM |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Gasoline C | Brazil | 5.3% | 3.2% | 3.2% | 3.9% |
| Gasoline C | State | 6.4% | 4.1% | 4.1% | 5.2% |
| Diesel | Brazil | 4.3% | 3.2% | 3.2% | 3.3% |
| Diesel | State | 6.0% | 4.7% | 4.7% | 5.0% |
| Hydrous ethanol | Brazil | 14.0% | 11.9% | 12.0% | 12.0% |
| Hydrous ethanol | State | 15.7% | 13.2% | 13.2% | 14.1% |

ETS cuts the benchmark's error by a quarter to two fifths for gasoline and diesel, and MinT makes every
level add up without losing accuracy, which is what a planning team needs. The global
gradient-boosting model does not beat ETS here: with 178 months per state there is not enough
history for it to learn more than the seasonal pattern. Ethanol stays hard at 12% to 13%, because
owners of flex cars switch fuel with the price ratio, which these models do not see.
:::

::: {.rh-section}
## Limits

The link from producer to distributor is not identified at weekly frequency in this window: state
tax changes from 2022 to 2025 and the rise of ethanol in gasoline from 27% to 30% move the
distribution price without the producer price, and since 2023 refinery prices change in rare steps.
Only its long-run share is reported, about 0.74 of a producer price change, which matches the share
of pure gasoline in gasoline C. The long-run pump coefficient is above one in most states, because
station margins widened over the period; it is not a markup on each cost change. The survey is a
sample of stations, not a census. The competition estimates are associations. The Databricks bundle
has not been deployed to a workspace from this repository; CI checks that it parses and that its
tasks point to working scripts.
:::

::: {.rh-section}
## Applied to your business

For a distributor, a chain of stations or a convenience retailer, the same pipeline runs on your
own prices and volumes: how fast your stations follow cost in each region, what your brand is worth
against each competitor set, and a sales forecast by station, city and state that adds up to the
plan. It starts with the <a href="../oquant.html#packages">Data &amp; AI Diagnostic</a> and runs in
your environment, on Databricks or elsewhere.
:::

## Code

```{=html}
<p>
<a class="rh-btn" href="https://github.com/rhozon/fuel-retail-analytics">github.com/rhozon/fuel-retail-analytics</a>
</p>
```

With Python 3.11 or later:

```bash
pip install -e ".[dev,track]"
pytest -v
python -I tools/fetch_anp_data.py ~/data/anp      # public data, no account
python -m fuelx.cli --out results --lake lake --track sqlite:///mlflow.db
databricks bundle deploy -t dev                   # with a Databricks workspace
```

The suite has **10 tests** and CI runs them on every push.
:::
